utterances.text: We are, Councilmember, looking also at how data flows.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And so we will certainly follow up with you on terms of what actually was surveyed and what did the samples look like.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Council Member Aviles asks whether MOIA is supporting NYC Public Schools in training staff on updated policies, not just leadership. Ali says MOIA is working closely with agencies on training timelines and ensuring policies do not sit on a shelf.
chapters.title: Council Member Aviles asks about NYC Public Schools training rollout

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: In terms of the work with the New York City Public Schools, again, thank you for, you know, being much more aggressive in this work with our city and our communities who are deeply struggling.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: In terms of the policy, the updated policy.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Are you supporting New York City Public Schools'effort in

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: actually what training down looks like, because we find that these policies stay stuck in OGCs or in leadership and very little attention being paid to how they actually go through the system.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: The one thing we want to avoid is a set of new policies that do the right thing and aren't actually being implemented.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And so we are working really closely with each of the agencies and including our partners at New York City Public Schools on timelines for their trainings and ensuring that these are completed.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: The updated policies that were rolled out prior to the first day of school were shared with principals before that first day of school.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And so we are pleased to know that there has been some progress.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: But part of the ongoing work with the IRC and the agencies is to ensure that this isn't something that sits on a shelf.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Yeah, all hands on deck.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: We'd love them to be able to validate that from janitorial service to kitchen staff to educators and paras.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Everyone in the building should know those policies.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And we often find they stay stuck at the principal level or leadership in the school.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: For that.

chapters.summary: Council Member Aviles asks about progress on Local Law 114 signage. Ali says MOIA created the signage and sent it to agencies, which are on track to post it by September 30th.
chapters.title: Council Member Aviles asks about Local Law 114 signage progress

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: In terms of the, I'd love to know if there's been any progress on local law 114 on the signage.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: I know that's not the focus of the hearing today, but I selfishly am going to ask.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: We were prepared, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: this question and wanted to make sure that you know we have pleased to say that we've actually made progress.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: We've created the signage and we've sent that out to agencies who are on track to have them posted no later than September 30th.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: I love that answer.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: I know how important it is to you.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: It's important to us, too.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Is it pretty?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: You know, it looks good.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: I'll be the judge of that.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: I did not design it, thankfully.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: I don't have those skills, but it looks good.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: I'm happy to share that with you as well.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Great, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: We'll follow up offline for sure.

chapters.summary: Council Member Aviles asks about use of the MOIA hotline amid public charge changes and ICE presence. Ali says calls have increased due to outreach and partnerships, and Lorena Lucero gives top-line numbers, including 154 individuals contacted through targeted TPS outreach.
chapters.title: Council Member Aviles asks about MOIA hotline usage and outreach

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: In terms of the hotline, obviously with the public charge change and just the constant surges of ice, well, potentially not

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: surges, but a consistent presence of ice across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: What has been your experience of the use of the hotline?

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Are you seeing any evidence of increases, positive engagement as a result of also the campaign to get information out?

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Just would like to hear some more about that.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Before I turn it over to my colleague who is equipped with numbers, I do want to just say that our partnership with our legal service providers, with our hotline providers has been really strong.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: We've put a tremendous amount of strain on them as well.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Given the climate that we are living in now, whether it's the expiration of TPS or an increase in ICE activity in our neighborhoods that we are also seeing and they are

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: fielding questions from the public on or public charge, there has been an increase in the number of calls.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And that is also due to the fact that there's been significant outreach.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And it's through partnerships with you all, frankly, and partnerships with council members when we are out in the community distributing our hotline information, people know that they can call and get some trusted, confidential legal support.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: So I'm going to turn it over to Lorena to share some top line numbers on who's calling and for what.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: I also knew you were going to ask about the hotline, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: But just to sort of say, we also have pivoted some of the work that the hotline is doing.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: So it's a bit more targeted.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: We had very targeted outreach for TPS, for example, clinics that were upcoming, as well as public charge.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: So there is a direct loop back to some of these providers so folks don't have to go in circles and they're getting direct service.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: I can tell you that with the launch of our targeted outreach for TPS for Haiti, at least 154 individuals were contacted for the hotline.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: On the weekend when our team was out canvassing in Little Haiti, we saw a very direct increase.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: I don't have that number in front of me, but I will get it to you.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: And that's what we've noticed.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: more that not only the mayor, who also shared the hotline, but also the direct touch point with community members has helped as well as some of our weekend hours.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: As you know, we're available and open one Saturday a month, and we have seen an increase, again, with the collaboration of some of the outreach that we're doing as well.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Great, thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Aviles raises the shortage of legal service providers physically present in the city and asks how the city is creatively addressing unmet need. She says she wants a deeper conversation about building the legal support pipeline.
chapters.title: Council Member Aviles raises shortage of legal service providers

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Chair, if I may just wrap last question or maybe a little bit of a comment.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Definitely heartened to hear the increased investment in making sure that the hotline is a functional hotline, that there are people on the other end of that hotline.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: I am interested in learning how we...

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Are collaborating around the very real issue that we do not have enough legal service providers

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: physically present in our city to meet the need and what kind of alternatives are we creatively thinking about around how to

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: address some of that unmet need.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: We may not get there entirely, but it feels like there's only so much we can do with a very finite element of resources.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So we'd love to have that deeper conversation with you all around what are the ways, how are we looking at the pipeline of legal support in our city to make sure that we continue to build into the future.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación moves to the Department of Probation and asks when it will institute limits on immigration status in pre-sentencing investigation reports and who will confirm. Ali says DOP has already instituted the limits, communicated them to executive staff, and reinforced them in trainings.
chapters.title: Chair Encarnación asks about Department of Probation limitations

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: So we are going to go into the Department of Probation now and questions around that.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: When will the Department of Probation Institute limitations on inclusion of information about immigrant status in presenting investigation reports?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And how will those be confirmed and who will be responsible for confirming this?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: DOP has already instituted these limitations.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Specifically, DOP communicated with executive staff outlining these limitations on including immigration status information in

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: pre-sentencing investigation reports, and they have reinforced both of this in their trainings in the academy and field trainings for probation officers that are assigned to investigations.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And were you involved in those?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: So as a member of the IRC, MOIA has worked on providing guidance on how to strengthen these protocols and others.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And just another point, I think we had mentioned this in our testimony, that we have established a regular process for the agency to submit reports under Local Law 228.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: So our interactions with the agency continue in that regard as well.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Great.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks whether DSS incident reports have been revised to ensure all shelter interactions are reported. Ali says DSS clarified that any interaction with non-local law enforcement must be labeled a Priority 1 incident and is reviewing reports through enhanced training.
chapters.title: Chair Encarnación asks about DSS incident reporting revisions

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And then I'll ask quickly.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: questions about DSS and then I'm going to pass it over to my colleague to ask some questions.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: In regards to DSS, have incident reports been revised to ensure that all incidents and interactions at DSS shelters are reported and what would be entailed in that reporting?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Yes, this has also been completed, and it really entails two main changes.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: DSS clarified that for all staff that any interaction with non-local law enforcement must be labeled a Priority 1 incident,

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: and that they are also continuing as an agency to review incidents and reports and ensure that no incident is missed through their enhanced training.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks about a recommendation regarding incorrect referrals to 26 Federal Plaza. Ali clarifies that DSS issued guidance that caseworkers should not refer individuals to 26 Federal Plaza but should connect them to immigration attorneys and legal services.
chapters.title: Chair Encarnación asks about DSS guidance on 26 Federal Plaza referrals

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I noticed that there was a recommendation that stated that guidance will be issued in response to an incorrect referral to 26 Federal Plaza.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Can you clarify what that means?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Yeah, DSS here issued clarifying and explicitly clarifying

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: guidance that caseworkers should not refer any individuals to 26 Federal Plaza, but instead they should be connecting individuals to an immigration attorney and legal services.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that.

chapters.summary: Council Member Joseph asks what steps the city is taking to aid people who may lose status in the future. Ali says MOIA works with Haitian Response Initiative partners, legal clinics, and the hotline to connect people to attorneys and help families plan next steps.
chapters.title: Council Member Joseph asks about aid for people losing status

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Councilmember?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Commissioner, always good to see you and your team.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you for that you do.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: A couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What option exists or what steps is

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: the city taking to aid people who may have lost status in the future, TPS or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: So on this front, I'm really pleased to say we've been working closely with our HRI partners to ensure that anyone who is at risk or has lost protections has access to legal services.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And so not only is a hotline available for individuals to call, but we have been standing up legal clinics in communities and through our partners to make sure that individuals are connected to an attorney and who can make an assessment if they have other forms of relief.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: The other thing that I think is really critical, and it pains me really to say this, is that in many circumstances, we are learning that there are very limited options for families.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And so we've been working with partners to train organizations on what does it mean to help a family really plan for what their next steps are.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: So it's really a combination of making sure, first and foremost, if there are legal options available, connecting individuals to those services, and then also making sure that there are additional resources that are available to families who are

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: especially vulnerable right now.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Well, thank you for also working with our non-for-profits to make this happen.

chapters.summary: Council Member Joseph asks whether the administration will conduct a similar audit or review in the future to learn lessons. Ali says there may not be a formal audit but the city has ongoing conversations with impacted people and service providers to pivot as needed.
chapters.title: Council Member Joseph asks about future audits and lessons learned

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Will the administration conduct an audit or review of similar scope in the future?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Audit as it relates to...

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: My previous question.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is there going to be an audit?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Are you going to look at this?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: There has to be less than...

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: learn, right?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: We don't just do policy to do policy.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: There is lessons to be learned.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: That is absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And I think that part, I don't know if it's a form of a formal audit, but these are ongoing conversations that we have with people who are most impacted on the ground and the service providers.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: They know what works and what does not work.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And if we need to pivot to other protections and other things that we need to offer families who are experiencing a loss of protection.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And I know, Councilmember, you will hold us accountable to that as well.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: No doubt.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: As you should.

chapters.summary: Council Member Joseph asks what audit tools the agencies and IRC use. Ali says the audit involved direct engagement with agencies reviewing every policy and protocol related to federal immigration enforcement interactions.
chapters.title: Council Member Joseph asks what audit tools agencies use

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What type of audit tools do the agencies include in the IRC utilize?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What kind of tools do you use?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: So the part of our audit, and this is included in our findings, is

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: engaging directly with the agencies who are reviewing every policy and protocol as it relates to any interaction that they have with federal immigration enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Some of those are agencies that are focused on immigration enforcement, like ICE, and then other agencies that are nontraditional.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And so what we're trying to do is make sure that agencies report every immigration agency interaction that they have.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And then we take it from there.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Joseph asks about the human capacity of agencies to respond and conduct audits. Ali says agencies have taken the work seriously and have been supportive, with no pushback so far.
chapters.title: Council Member Joseph asks about agency human capacity for audits

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: The most famous question, and I think Councilmember Aviles, what human capacity do these agencies have to respond and conduct audits?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Yeah, this is really important.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And I think that it's been really reflective in the level of

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: cooperation from agencies, that agencies are taking this work really seriously as well.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: They understand the city's role in protecting immigrant communities and preserving service delivery.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And so, you know, this is something that is an ongoing conversation with agencies, but I'm pleased to say that everyone has been really supportive and engaging in this process, and we haven't had any issues or pushback.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Good to hear.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Good to hear.

chapters.summary: Council Member Joseph asks what staff are instructed to do when armed and masked federal agents enter shelters without permission. Ali says DSS revised protocols and flow charts, and frontline staff should photograph warrants and let legal counsel determine whether entry is allowed.
chapters.title: Council Member Joseph asks about armed ICE shelter incident protocols

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: In the audit, finding included description of a February 2025 situation in which armed and masked agencies enter the shelter facility without permission of agency staff.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What are we instructing staff to do in such situation if there's a training and such policies?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Because I know even when they were asking questions for them to identify themselves, they just pushed into the shelter and just went about.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What protocols are in place?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: I think that that's a very important question.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: DSS has issued and revised protocols for frontline agency staff and updated a flow chart that's going to be posted at every shelter on what to do if they face that encounter.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And right now they're working to incorporate and strengthen those best practices in its trainings.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: I think the most important and critical piece here is that frontline staff know that they are not alone.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: loan in making a determination if an agency is coming in, if they are allowed to enter the facility.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And by that, I mean if someone comes in and presents themselves as a federal enforcement agency and says, I have a warrant, you know, they will take that warrant and not make an assessment.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Is it just a warrant?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Are they allowed entry?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: They will take a photograph, flag that for their legal counsel, and only the legal counsel will be making that determination on who enters.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: So there are a series of protocols that have been put in place to prevent that and really protect the frontline staff and make sure that they're equipped to protect anyone who is in the shelter.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: But we've seen how aggressive ICE has been on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So I don't know how much pushback.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Sometimes they can do.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So we have to probably revisit that conversation.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And this is part of the IRC's work in continuing to engage the agencies because what we're seeing now and what we anticipate is that immigration enforcement will continue to evolve.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And so that forces us and requires us to continuously look at our policies as well.

chapters.summary: Council Member Joseph asks how many times federal agents have entered New York City facilities without permission. Ali says that is a great question and MOIA will follow up with the number.
chapters.title: Council Member Joseph asks how often federal agents entered facilities

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Chair, I just have one more question.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How many times have federal agents entered New York City operative facilities without permission or despite a lack of permission?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: That is a great question, and we can follow up with you on that.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: That would be great.

chapters.summary: Council Member Joseph asks how MOIA is working with Project Open Arms and NYC Public Schools to protect students, including legal steps if students are detained. Lorena Lucero says MOIA speaks with Project Open Arms weekly and coordinates on legal services and elevated cases.
chapters.title: Council Member Joseph asks about Project Open Arms and student detention

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And then my other question is, how is Moya working with Open Arms in New York City Public School?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: You know that was coming.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And to make sure that...

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: If our students are detained, what are the legal steps?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: The council has been very supportive, and what are the legal steps in place?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And have there been any ice-taking of any of our students recently?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Do you want to talk about Project Open Arms?

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: So we, I speak to them every week, and that's true.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: And we have been working very collaboratively.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: The commissioner mentioned on top that even with the rollout of some of the protocols at schools, we were working closely with them.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: We continue to collaborate on the legal services front and coordinate if cases are elevated.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: As from the top of my head, I can't give you if there was a number or something like that.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: I haven't either.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: But I'm happy to circle back, but we are working with them.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: Again, we thank council for the foresight in supporting that initiative with Project Open Arms in particular because it has added some capacity, so we appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is there any collaboration with the door?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: The organization, the door, because they also do that work around young people and especially young people who are in care.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: We work with them through iCare as well, through the iCare Coalition and some of the work that we do with unaccompanied minors.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I look forward to more conversations.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks whether protocols and trainings include detailed reporting to the Attorney General's office when incidents occur. Ali says it is part of Local Law 228 reporting and the city encourages over-inclusive reporting of any interaction that may relate to immigration enforcement.
chapters.title: Chair Encarnación asks about reporting incidents to the AG's office

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Actually, in part of the...

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Protocols and trainings that you all have, is there a detailed about reporting when an incident like this happenings, for example, to like the AG's office, that there is now a system in place that they can report?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Is that part of the training?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: protocol so people know what to do if someone does push past them and go forward?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: That is part of our local law 228 reporting and part of the enhanced protocol there.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And I feel like I've referenced, I continue to reference this because I think it's a really important point, is the over-inclusive reporting that is now being encouraged.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Any interaction, if it smells like an immigration, we want to make sure that that is reflective in the reports that are shared with MOIA.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And so we are looking, that is one way to capture these incidents, and that is one way that these incidents have been captured in these reports as well.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And so in those trainings, it does include like what they should be detailing, taking information on pictures, if anything, videos or anything like that, that all can be submitted as part of the reporting.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: I will have to get back to you on what exact information, if it includes videos or other footage.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Yeah, we can follow up on that.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Great.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks how aligned trainings are for school safety officers and school staff, since school safety falls under NYPD. Ali says training applies to school safety agents and frontline staff, but MOIA will follow up on who exactly trains school safety agents.
chapters.title: Chair Encarnación asks about school safety officer training alignment

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And then also just thinking about the public schools and knowing that school safety falls under NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And so are they getting how different or aligned are the trainings for school safety officers to actual staff in the school building?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: So the training applies to school safety agents and all frontline staff in New York City public schools.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And so that comes, so school safety agents are being trained through the Department of Education, not through the armed.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: The NYPD?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: On this, we'll have to defer to our New York City Public Schools team, but we can also follow up and get clarity on who is exactly training the school safety agents.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Perfect.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Sometimes those who don't talk.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: So we want to make sure that everybody is on the same line.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación moves to DOHMH and asks about post-incident protocols. Ali says MOIA and the IRC are working with DOHMH on protocols including notification to individuals and counsel, with a target date of October 30th.
chapters.title: Chair Encarnación asks about DOHMH post-incident protocols

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Now switching over to DOHMH, which snaps for them for participating in this willingly.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I know in your opening statement, you'd mentioned that they have already developed and issued

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And we're finalizing their post-incident protocols.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Are you talking about H&H or that's for H&H?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: H&H or DOH?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: DOHMH, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Yes, so MOYA is working with the IRC and DOHMH.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: They are developing protocols, including notification to individuals and their counsel when appropriate with its Office of General Counsel and aiming for a target date.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: That protocol, we're hoping, is finalized by October 30th.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: October 30th.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: So it's later.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: I was going to say later this month.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Later next month.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Almost.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks about DOHMH's process to audit facility signage. Ali says DOHMH has new signage under review and plans installation by October 30th in collaboration with MOIA.
chapters.title: Chair Encarnación asks about DOHMH facility signage audit

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: There was also some mention of developing a process to audit facility signage.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: So what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: So DOHMH has a new sign.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: a new signage that's currently under review.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: This is signage that is posted in their facilities.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: They're planning for installation of this new signage that is underway.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: I think the aim for that target date is also October 30th for implementation.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Also in collaboration with you all.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Correct.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks when NYPD will institute its protocol for notifying the operations division of civil immigration requests and who confirms it. Ali says NYPD established the protocol and the IRC is supporting and confirming implementation.
chapters.title: Chair Encarnación asks about NYPD civil immigration notification protocol

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Okay, in terms of the NYPD, when will the NYPD institute their protocol for notification to the operations division of any requests for information or otherwise in connection with civil immigration enforcement?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And who is responsible for confirming when this is instituted?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: The NYPD has established this protocol for any requests for information or otherwise in connection to civil immigration enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: This is part of the ongoing work within the NYPD to institutionalize this policy, this protocol through policy, and the IRC is working to support and confirm when this policy is implemented.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: So this is work through the committee.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: So the IRC as a whole is responsible for confirming what it is.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And there are also, will adapt enhanced protocols requiring supervisory and legal review.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: This protocol in particular is something that the PD is continuing to work on, and it will soon release this new protocol.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: soon as in before the year is up or?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: It's on track to release the new protocols that assess this.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And we're working really closely to, you know, get closer to releasing this.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks about NYPD's protocol for 911 calls related to federal immigration authorities and who confirms it. Ali says the IRC works with agencies on implementation plans and NYPD has begun implementing the 911 protocol.
chapters.title: Chair Encarnación asks about NYPD 911 call protocol

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And the same question as it pertains to 911 calls.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And related to the presence of federal immigration authorities or immigration matters.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Who is, again, is the IRC, again, responsible for confirming that that protocol is established?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Yes, that is a work that we're ongoing work with us and each agency on their implementation plan.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And on this, you know, I'm happy to share that the PD has begun implementation of this particular protocol in response to 911 calls as they relate to immigration enforcement or immigration activities overall.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: So outside of the IRC, what formal or informal lines of communication exists between MOIA and NYPD for purposes of this kind of reporting or just information sharing and its impact on immigrant communities?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Yeah, we continue to work across agencies and outside of the IRC.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: You know, we have the interagency task force that MOIA also conducts that includes, you know, all 40 plus city agencies where we share best practices, where we flag any incidents and information.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: So we have, you know, good.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: communication across agencies, including the NYPD.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks whether NYPD completed its email audit of task force officers. Ali says the email audit is complete and under review, and NYPD is now in compliance with outstanding reporting requirements under Local Laws 10-178 and 14-154.
chapters.title: Chair Encarnación asks about NYPD email audit and reporting compliance

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Did they complete their email audit that was, I guess it was slated to be completed by the end of 2026?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Yes, the NYPD did conduct an email audit of the task force officers, I believe that's what you're referencing, to ensure that there is compliance with local law.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: That email audit is complete and is currently under review.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And will there be a cadence of additional audits in terms of those email exchanges?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Related to the cadence, I'm going to defer to our colleagues at the NYPD on that.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Gotcha.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: So it's essentially the required piece is done, and so anything would be...

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Reviewed.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Gotcha.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And have they complied with the outstanding reporting requirements under 10-178 and 14-154?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Yes, I'm happy to report that the PD is now in compliance with those outstanding reporting requirements.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: They've also completed a new revision to the patrol guide on elevating civil immigration detainer requests to appropriate supervisors and review and determine any action that needs to be taken.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Perfect.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación moves to H&H and asks whether it will work with MOIA to implement its five key recommendations. Ali says MOIA as part of the IRC will support H&H, and H&H has voluntarily committed to submitting Local Law 228 reports within privacy limits.
chapters.title: Chair Encarnación asks about H&H recommendations and reporting

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Now H&H.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: So H&H developed five key recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Will they be working with MOYA to implement those recommendations moving forward?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Yeah, so MOYA.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: as part of the IRC is going to be working with H&H by supporting and guiding them on their implementation of these recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Including the reporting requirements in 10-178?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: H&H has voluntarily committed to submitting reports in the next local law 228 reporting cycle within, of course, the parameters of HIPAA and other legal privacy requirements.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks about Operation Rotten Apple and whether MOIA tracked the summer surge of ICE agents. Ali says MOIA closely monitors enforcement trends and tracks ICE interactions with city agencies under Local Law 228, while also monitoring national trends and community reports.
chapters.title: Chair Encarnación asks about Operation Rotten Apple and ICE surge tracking

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Now, in terms of non-local law enforcement in New York City, I know the city found that the Department of Homeland Security

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: was operating something called Operation Rotten Apple and took place this summer, which confirmed the uptick of ICE agents across the city.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Were you tracking the surge as more?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: So we've seen an increase in immigration enforcement activities across the city,

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: which we know have had a really significant impact on immigrant communities and its heightened concerns amongst New Yorkers and neighbors alike.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: MOIA does closely monitor these trends and their impact.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: MOIA, along with our partners at the IRC, also track ICE enforcement as it relates to how they interact with city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: That's where we have visibility and that's where we have authority.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And specifically under local law 228, MOIA and other agencies are required.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: to track, as you previously mentioned, and report any requests, any interactions.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And then more broadly, I'll say that we are monitoring trends both in New York City and really across the country and remain in close communication with state partners, with our advocates, with community organizations,

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: mutual aid groups who are on the ground and really are the eyes and ears for different communities to understand what is actually happening and how best can cities respond.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks whether MOIA performed targeted outreach in areas with spikes. Ali says MOIA's community engagement team canvasses impacted neighborhoods, distributes Know Your Rights information, and works with partner agencies; Lorena Lucero adds they partner with other city offices for broader reach.
chapters.title: Chair Encarnación asks about targeted outreach during surges

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And I'm assuming that part of that was also performing targeted outreach in the areas where you saw spikes and surges.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: We have a community engagement team that we deploy in neighborhoods that are impacted.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: They'll go out a few days of the week and canvas neighborhoods, give out know your rights information, talk to small businesses, and making sure that if anyone is one directly impacted, has information on how to access our immigration legal support hotline,

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: but also is equipped with know your rights information.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: What do you do if you encounter ICE at work or at home?

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: I'll just add here, if I may, Chair, that MOIA has worked with our interagency partners.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: So we are actively partnering with the Office of Mass Engagement, the Mayor's Office of Public Engagement, SBS, and DCWP to leverage some of their folks so we can have a larger reach around.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: You guys are so good.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Every time I'm about to ask about if you need more resources, you tell me about all the resources that you implore to get the work done.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Because I'm assuming that when there is a surge and there's an increase of need for people to be out and actually reaching folks.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: It's an all hands on deck moment.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And we're really grateful for our partners.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: You know, one thing I think Lorena stopped short is of kind of sharing the impact that these partnerships are actually making.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: You know, we've conducted just since March, since I joined, 30 canvassing events and days of actions across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: We've distributed over 8,000 printed materials and engaged 650 businesses.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And all of that work is not possible, one, without the incredible team at MOIA that I am fortunate to work with every day, but also that deep partnership with different parts of city government.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks how the IRC will function during future surges and whether it will expand. Ali says the IRC will continue as a coordinating body to monitor federal enforcement and policy changes and support agencies serving immigrant New Yorkers.
chapters.title: Chair Encarnación asks about the future role of the IRC

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I had another question that just went out of my head.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: But I guess, what do you see the function for IRC as continued surges or future surges come?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Where do you see them playing the similar role?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Do you see IRC expanding to include additional people?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: What do you feel like for the future of the IRC?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that it's critical to sort of really be grounded in, you know, why the IRC was established and for what purpose.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And it's really to, you know, serve as a coordinating body, right, to respond to the federal actions that are affecting New York City residents, to monitor the federal enforcement activity, and then to provide support

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: to city agencies and making sure that they have what they need to deliver services to immigrant New Yorkers and that they are also protected and have the support that they need to do this work.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: So that work is ongoing.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: I think that there are significant changes and increases that are happening on the federal level in terms of policy.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: So it's not just enforcement activity, but we are seeing significant policy changes, public charge, changes to

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: other policies that have real impacts in New York City and are felt on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And so we're really...

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: pleased that we have thought partners within the IRC to help track and monitor those developments, but also work with us to deliver information to New Yorkers who might be impacted.

utterances.text: So those reports have been published?

utterances.text: Yesterday.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Of course, in alignment with other city agencies and within for H&H, within the parameters of HIPAA and FERPA and all the other legal privacy requirements as well.

chapters.title: Chair Encarnación asks about detainer reporting standardization

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Now, the report also notes that NYPD and the Department of Probations are not currently required to disaggregate the number of civil immigration detainers lodged by conviction status

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: and or possible match in federal terrorist screening database, whereas DOC is required to do so.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I know the report recommends that these three agencies standardize their reportings.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: So have NYPD and DOP agreed to adopt this recommendation?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: So the NYPD and DOP will, the short answer is yes, and they will report on civil immigration detainers broken down by conviction status

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: and or possible match in a federal terrorist screening database.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: And this already aligns with what DOC is currently doing.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And in the IRC's view, and you may not want to speak for it,

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: for the full IRC, but as a member of the IRC, or you may know, would this discrepancy require a legislative fix?

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: On that, I'll defer to the council regarding any future legislation, but the agencies here are in compliance.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: The report also states that NYPD, DOC, DOP are required to submit the quarterly detainer reports.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: So that is happening, you said, right?

utterances.text: And all three agencies have agreed to the frequency of reporting.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: How many people have called the hotline for connection to specifically immigration legal services?

utterances.text: That's the top issue as to why people call.

utterances.text: So that information I wouldn't have because we don't collect people's, you know, personal identifying information.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: But I can say that the hotline has been shared.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: New New Yorkers, old New Yorkers, and that number has been shared with people so they can access legal services.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: But we just don't track that.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Yeah.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación asks how MOIA defines a surge neighborhood and how often outreach happens. Lucero says they go by council district, respond to reports from advocates and partners, and conduct at least one outreach event per week, sometimes more during crises like Haiti TPS.
chapters.title: Chair Encarnación asks about outreach in surge neighborhoods

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And I appreciate some of your details in talking about how

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: neighborhoods that are experiencing frequent ice activity, you know, what kind of things are deployed there, some of the agencies that have been tasked to help.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: You mentioned mass engagement, W.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: DCWP, SBS, all great agencies.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: In the surrounding neighborhoods or neighborhoods that are surrounding them, do you see it?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Like, what is the radius, should I say, of what classifies as a neighborhood that is experiencing a surge?

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: Well, we go by district.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: So similar to the council's district map, that's sort of what we do.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: When we hear, and we could hear this from advocates, we can hear this from the news, we can hear it from other agency partners if there is a nice spotting, for example.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: I would say that the surge in New York has looked different than across the country, right?

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: maybe in LA, so very targeted to a specific area and location.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: In New York, it's a bit different.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: They're a bit more scattered.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: So when we hear about them, we do share that with our outreach staff and equip them with information.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: What we want to do is to be on the ground as quickly as we can to share some of the legal service forward-facing material and information.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: We try to target areas where we know people will be, so train stations, business corridors, for example.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: And then we try to match it up so we can get to people like workers, right?

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: So after six o'clock, for example.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: And that's the way that we do it.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: I will say that we have partnered with city council members.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: I think we've partnered with you at least in one event because you're also the eyes and ears.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: And I think that's an open invitation to work with us, given how close you are with the districts.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: And you might know corners that we might just not by not having that insight in some of those council districts.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: But that's a bit how that works.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And how often do those outreach surges, I'll call them, happen?

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: We do an outreach event at least once a week, and sometimes two or three.

utterances.speaker: Lorena Lucero
utterances.text: And I would say that when the news came down from TPS connected to Haiti, we were in Little Haiti that week at least three times in one week.

chapters.summary: Chair Encarnación thanks MOIA for its work and says EO 13 was helpful but only the beginning. She says the committee will follow up on implementation of findings and recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And we really look forward to seeing how these findings, these recommendations are all implemented and how more come out throughout that process.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And so we'll be following up.

chapters.title: Chair Encarnación asks about Commissioner Ali's ongoing IRC role

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And then just lastly, in terms of, you know,

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: your role in commissioner and the IRC, is this something that you see as a, I know you mentioned that there was a chair who was, who's sharing the first deputy mayor is chairing that.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: What do you see as ongoing, um, your role being how significant in, in this,

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: particular thing because of course I want you to run it.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: You know, given the climate and given the sort of fast changing nature of immigration enforcement and, you know, on activities on the ground and in policy, I think it's really critical the role that the IRC continues to play.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: I think it's actually extremely important and to underscore having, you know, senior level city hall staff and team and leaders, frankly, guiding this work is what is, to me,

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: communicates that this is a serious issue for the mayor.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: Having the first deputy mayor be present in these meetings to help guide the conversation is an indication that we are serious about protecting New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: So this work is ongoing.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: I'm really pleased to work.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: I feel really privileged to work with.

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: with the FDM, with his team, with the chief counsel, having the support of the law department, and the countless staff, frankly, that make this work happen to show that

utterances.speaker: Faiza Ali
utterances.text: we are serious when it comes to protecting immigrant New Yorkers and families.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

chapters.summary: Isabel Ortega Romero says New York City is home to 3.1 million immigrants who make up 38% of the population and paid $74.8 billion in taxes in 2024. She says immigrants live in fear and that the audit revealed many city agencies were not complying with sanctuary laws.
chapters.title: Isabel Ortega Romero testifies on immigrant contributions and sanctuary compliance

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: There we go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Encarnacion and members of the committee for holding this hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: My name is Isabel Ortega Romero, and I'm here representing the Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: New York City is home to 3.1 million immigrants, 38% of the city's population.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: The city is built by immigrants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: Immigrants comprise 43% of our workforce, and in 2024 alone, immigrant New Yorkers paid $74.8 billion in taxes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: However, immigrants are far more than the labor they provide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: They are our neighbors, friends, community members and leaders, and family.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: New York City is a sanctuary city, but its people are living in fear that going outside might lead to permanent separation from their loved ones.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: ICE arrested more people this July than in any other month during President Trump's second term.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: Recently, the administration's audit of city agencies revealed that many city agencies were not in compliance with sanctuary city laws.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: We commend the mayor for conducting this audit and agree with its recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: And we need more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: Meaningful and reliable oversight of agencies'compliance with sanctuary city laws must be independent and ongoing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: Because sanctuary city laws are only as strong as their enforcement, and allowing city agencies to unlawfully cooperate with ICE erodes trust in city government.

chapters.summary: Isabel Ortega Romero recommends forming an independent commission to audit and enforce sanctuary compliance, drafting penalties for violations, and creating disciplinary procedures. She also says Borough President Reynoso strongly supports Resolution 626 and S.4814 for Haiti TPS.
chapters.title: Isabel Ortega Romero recommends independent sanctuary oversight and TPS support

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: For these reasons, we recommend the following.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: Form an independent commission to audit, monitor, and enforce compliance with sanctuary city laws.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: This commission would conduct quarterly audits to thoroughly examine noncompliance and misconduct and would hold city agencies accountable for violations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: Draft legislation creating penalties for violations of sanctuary city laws.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: Recommendations are not enough to ensure that agencies will abide by the law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: City Council should establish mandatory disciplinary action, fines, procedures for removing officers, employees, and agency leadership, and other enforcement mechanisms for repeat violations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: The intent of these recommendations is to ensure that city agencies abide by city law designed to protect the safety and rights of all New Yorkers regardless of national origin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: We can only prevent federal outreach by ensuring local agencies abide by the law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: Lastly, Borough President Reynoso's

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: strongly supports Resolution 626, which requires the Secretary of Homeland Security to designate Haiti for temporary protected status.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: We hope that S-4814 passes so that our Haitian community can access health care, education, and employment without legal risk.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: Thank you again for holding this hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: We look forward to continuing to work with you to ensure that city government advances justice, promotes public trust, and honors the laws that protect immigrants who call this city home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Isabel Ortega Romero
utterances.text: Thank you.
