chapters.summary: Stephanie Delia of Little Haiti BK says over half a million Haitian TPS recipients lost status on July 27, 2026, and there are not enough immigration lawyers. She calls for more pro se services, preparedness planning, guardianship orders, and ways to protect assets if people are removed.
chapters.title: Stephanie Delia of Little Haiti BK testifies on pro se services and preparedness

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Delia
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Encarnacion and New York City Council Immigration Committee for hearing us today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Delia
utterances.text: My name is Stephanie Delia, and I'm the Executive Director of Little Haiti BK.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Delia
utterances.text: On July 27, 2026, over half a million Haitian TPS recipients lost status and over 100,000

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Delia
utterances.text: Syrian immigrant TPS recipients lost status.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Delia
utterances.text: We know by those sheer numbers alone that there are not enough immigration lawyers to represent each and every single one of them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Delia
utterances.text: In response to that, I think the city has a duty to start to focus substantially more on pro se services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Delia
utterances.text: If we cannot be there with them, at least give them the tools, the information, and the confidence to support themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Delia
utterances.text: I used to work with QD Citizenship Now, and I know personally that they are one of the best at doing this work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Delia
utterances.text: Little Haiti BK is partnering with them to provide legal services so that people could be prepared to represent themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Delia
utterances.text: Pro se, as many of the former TPS recipients are receiving notices to appear to show up in court.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Delia
utterances.text: We have seen by the prior reports that some of the agencies, unfortunately, are sharing information, and so some of the former TPS recipients attending court are not safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Delia
utterances.text: In addition to just immigration services, I cannot stress the importance of preparedness planning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Delia
utterances.text: Specifically, it is important that people protect their children, protect their money, come up with an emergency plan so that they could help protect themselves, and get their documents in order so that if they are picked up by ICE unexpectedly,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Delia
utterances.text: an attorney who is prepared to assist them can get the documents quickly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Delia
utterances.text: We know that this administration is transporting parents or people to other states, and so to the extent somebody gets picked up in New York and ends up going to Louisiana, we want to ensure that if they have

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Delia
utterances.text: any of the proper orders, guardianship orders filed for their children, that at one point they could be reunited and families do not get separated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Delia
utterances.text: Lastly, when it comes to protecting their money, a lot of the Haitian TPS recipients have been in America for a very long time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Delia
utterances.text: They own businesses, they own property, they have made a living here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Delia
utterances.text: They have a huge portion of this community in the healthcare industry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Delia
utterances.text: They have pensions, they have 401k plans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Delia
utterances.text: Some of them have small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Delia
utterances.text: And I think it's very important that the city starts to consider manners to ensure that they are able to protect some of their funds if they are unexpectedly removed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Delia
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

chapters.summary: Lady Zela Rosa of La Colmena describes ICE enforcement on Staten Island days after a Mexican Independence Day parade and says staff witnessed an officer threatening a child. She calls for concrete investment in trusted community-based organizations to receive reports and connect people to services.
chapters.title: Lady Zela Rosa of La Colmena testifies on Staten Island ICE activity

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lady Zela Rosa
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Sharon Carnation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lady Zela Rosa
utterances.text: My name is Lady Zela Rosa, and I'm the advocacy coordinator at La Colmena, where I'm a nonprofit community-based organization working with day laborers, domestic workers, and other low-wage immigrant workers in Staten Island

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lady Zela Rosa
utterances.text: through organizing education, culture, and equitable economic development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lady Zela Rosa
utterances.text: On September 13, on Port Richmond Avenue in Staten Island, we celebrated Mexican Independence Day with a colorful and vibrant parade.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lady Zela Rosa
utterances.text: And just a few days later, ICE enforcement activity took place on those same streets, terrorizing members of our community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lady Zela Rosa
utterances.text: Our staff was there, and they witnessed a nice officer threatening a child.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lady Zela Rosa
utterances.text: These are not stories that we hear from the news.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lady Zela Rosa
utterances.text: As local organizations, we are learning about these incidents directly from the people in our community who are experiencing them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lady Zela Rosa
utterances.text: This is why community-based organizations are so important in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lady Zela Rosa
utterances.text: Organizations like La Colmena play a critical role in building trust, educating workers about their rights, and connecting community members with appropriate legal, mental health, and other support services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lady Zela Rosa
utterances.text: We are very receiving calls from community members about what they're experiencing and what they should do when they encounter immigration enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lady Zela Rosa
utterances.text: While strengthening NYPD protocols is an important step forward, we also have to recognize the reality on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lady Zela Rosa
utterances.text: Some immigrant workers and families may feel safer reaching out to a trusted community organization than directly to a government agency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lady Zela Rosa
utterances.text: This is why the city must make concrete investments in communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lady Zela Rosa
utterances.text: community-based organizations that are very trusted by immigrant communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lady Zela Rosa
utterances.text: We could receive and document reports, connect people with legal assistance and other services, and follow up with community members and help ensure that incidents do not go unaddressed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lady Zela Rosa
utterances.text: Executive Order 13 order was an important step towards strengthening New York City's sanctuary protections, but protections on paper are not enough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lady Zela Rosa
utterances.text: Those protections must be understandable, accessible, and meaningful in practice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lady Zela Rosa
utterances.text: City protections only work if people know about them, trust them, and feel safe enough to use them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lady Zela Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you for your continuous commitment to the people of New York City and for allowing me to testify.

chapters.summary: Nazia Fiazi of Health Justice for New York says protections must be felt in hospitals, shelters, schools, and agencies. She calls for clear multilingual information, regular front-facing employee training, and ways to measure whether policies are working, especially for immigrant women.
chapters.title: Nazia Fiazi of Health Justice for New York testifies on accessible protections

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: Good morning, members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: My name is Nazia Fiazi.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: I'm a steering member of the Health Justice for New York, and I'm currently a grad student studying data analytics and public health policy at Mount Sinai.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: I'm here with also a committee member, Steve Arbog.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: My background has been in neuroscience research and management.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: I say this because it's relevant to what I'm about to say.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: I'm also here from a personal experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: I was once an immigrant myself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: So I understand the challenges immigrants face is not always visible in a policy document or statistic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: Sometimes they are simply the fear and uncertainty that come with interacting with institutions you don't always know that you can trust.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: That is why I believe that protecting immigrant New Yorkers has to mean more than creating policies on paper.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: These protections have to be something people can actually feel when they walk into a hospital or a shelter, a school, or a city agency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: For many immigrants, there's already a fear of interacting with the government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: When you add the fear of immigration enforcement, that fear can become a barrier to getting help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: Someone may be sick but hesitate to go to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: A parent may need assistance for their child but be afraid to ask for it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: Someone experiencing domestic violence and mental health crisis or another urgent situation may worry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: about what information will be collected and where it could go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: From a public health perspective, this matters because fear can become a barrier to care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: I believe the city should focus not only on whether agencies have the correct policies, but on whether New Yorkers can actually understand those protections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: I would like to see clear multilingual information about immigrant rights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: Available where people receive services that are not buried on hard-to-navigate government websites.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: I would also like to see regular training for city employees that are front-facing with immigrants so that people will receive the same protections regardless of which agency or employee they interact with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: I believe the city should be able to have ways to measure whether these policies are doing what they say they are, how effective they are working for the people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: We need to understand if people are avoiding health care and other essential services because they're afraid.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: Are agencies consistently following these procedures that are already in place and what gaps are missing?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: In addition, I want us to think about this through the experience of immigrant women.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: During my times as a case manager at a family shelter, it was predominantly immigrant women who represented their families.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: These women were seeking health care for pregnancy, domestic violence, mental health, and other pertinent services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: A lot of times I had tough conversations with these folks about doing what's best for them while trying to calm their feels about putting themselves and their families at risk by getting their basic needs taken care of.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: My message today is simple.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: A right that people are afraid to exercise is not truly accessible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: New York City has an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: to make its protections practical, understandable, and accessible to the people who need them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nazia Fiazi
utterances.text: Thank you for allowing me to testify today.

chapters.summary: Dr. Steve Auerbach of Health Justice for New York says the audit shows sanctuary laws need actual enforcement and consequences for violators, including DOC and NYPD. He supports S.4814, calls on Senator Schumer to whip votes, and urges pressure on private hospitals to obey laws.
chapters.title: Dr. Steve Auerbach of Health Justice for New York calls for enforcement

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: Hi, I'm Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: Steve Auerbach with Health and Justice for New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: Thank you for having us again in front of this committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: Wish it wasn't so necessary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: We have supported in the past on 2025 in 214, 1268, 1272, and 1412.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: And earlier this year, 55 and 261.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: And of course, the New York Trust Act and 395 and 396, which I think we'll be getting new numbers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: We support all of those.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: And of course, the mayor's executive order 13.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: What has been shown with the audit is that there needs to be actual enforcement, including consequences, for persons who violate existing sanctuary laws and the executive order.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: That needs to include...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: And it is politically tough, but it needs to include if you're going to actually have law enforcement equal under the law for everybody,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: members of DOC, NYPD, et cetera, who violate existing statute and executive order.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: Number one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: Number two, we support, of course, S-4814.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: We call on our joint Senator Schumer to use his powers majority.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: leader to whip the handful of Democrats who have not signed on to it, including in our neighbor, Connecticut.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: We also co-wrote with Attorney General James and feel very proud of the New York State Law Legislature Safe Access to Care Act that was mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: It is carried by Rivera S10494 and AM Forest A11537.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: And we would call on both passage in the New York State Legislature and perhaps a copycat legislation at the city level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: And finally, I really want to call upon, and this is my main message, I want to call upon the city council and the mayor to use

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: whatever means necessary, whether it's the bully pulpit or calling stakeholders together to involve the...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: Private voluntary hospitals, whether it's individually or through their group, the Greater New York Hospital Association, Hospital Association, State of New York, to also obey these laws.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: Senior management at some of those hospitals, including their boards of directors, include MAGA supporters, and they have been very reticent

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: to follow New York City and New York state law, and there needs to be consequences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: There are levers, including zoning, taxes, and licensing of facilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: licensing that can be brought to bear if they're non-cooperative.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: We need enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Auerbach
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación

chapters.summary: Amanda Powers of NYC Anti-Violence Project says AVP serves LGBTQ+ and HIV-positive survivors of violence, including immigrants. She describes a transgender client in solitary confinement in an all-male ICE detention center and urges passage of the Trust Act and Intros 395 and 396.
chapters.title: Amanda Powers of NYC Anti-Violence Project testifies on LGBTQ immigrant survivors

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Powers
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Encarnacion and the committee for holding this public hearing to address Executive Order 13.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Powers
utterances.text: My name is Amanda Powers, and I am a legal fellow at the New York City Anti-Violence Project, or AVP.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Powers
utterances.text: AVP provides critical, holistic support and legal services to LGBTQ plus and HIV positive survivors of violence, including many immigrant survivors of violence in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Powers
utterances.text: Today, in addition to discussing EO13, I offer my voice on behalf of the queer immigrant survivors of violence who AVP serves to urge you to pass critical legislation that will allow immigrant New Yorkers who have survived violence to feel safe interacting

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Powers
utterances.text: with city government, specifically the New York City Trust Act, Intro 209, as well as former Intros 395 and 396.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Powers
utterances.text: And thank you, Chair Encarnacion, for sharing your ongoing support for 395 and 396.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Powers
utterances.text: At AVP, our immigrant clients live in constant fear of ICE detention or deportation because of the devastating reality that for many LGBTQ plus immigrants,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Powers
utterances.text: Deportation is a death sentence, and ICE detention centers are sites of anti-LGBTQ plus violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Powers
utterances.text: One of our clients, a transgender woman who came to New York City seeking safety from the transphobic violence in her home country, is currently sitting in solitary confinement in an all-male immigration detention center in Louisiana.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Powers
utterances.text: In detention, she has experienced transphobic attacks and violent harassment from guards and been denied access to necessary medical care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Powers
utterances.text: Before her detention, she survived violent rape in New York City, but did not report it to the police because she was afraid that doing so would lead to her being targeted by ICE.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Powers
utterances.text: Now, months later, AVP has helped her report the crime from inside ICE detention in Louisiana.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Powers
utterances.text: Her reality is the reality that LGBTQ plus immigrant New Yorkers understandably fear they will experience if their information is shared with ICE.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Powers
utterances.text: This fear is holding back AVP clients from interacting with city agencies at many levels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Powers
utterances.text: AVP operates a crisis hotline for queer survivors of violence in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Powers
utterances.text: So we hear every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Powers
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Powers
utterances.text: We hear every day from community members who are experiencing abuse and exploitation, but who feel that they cannot seek help from city agencies because they believe that government contact will lead them to further violence at the hands of ICE.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Powers
utterances.text: We hear stories from hotline users and clients about how this fear of ICE prevents domestic violence victims from seeking government resources to enable leaving their abusers or from relying on the city's shelter system after fleeing abuse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Powers
utterances.text: And how it's keeping LGBTQ plus survivors of violence from pursuing their winnable immigration cases because they believe that interacting with any government entity will make them a target for federal immigration enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Powers
utterances.text: Passing the New York City Trust Act and Intros 395 and 396 are important steps toward rebuilding trust with immigrant New Yorkers, and specifically with the LGBTQ plus survivors of violence who we work with at AVP.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amanda Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today.

summary: The Committee on Immigration held an oversight hearing on Executive Order 13 of 2026 and its audit of city agency compliance with sanctuary laws, with testimony from MOIA Commissioner Faiza Ali and public advocates.
Chair Elsie Encarnación and Council Members Aviles and Joseph questioned the administration on IRC operations, agency protocols, data sharing, training, reporting, and implementation timelines.

The committee also heard Resolution 626, sponsored by Council Member Farah Louis, calling on the U.S. Senate to pass S.4814 to designate Haiti for Temporary Protected Status, with extensive public testimony supporting Haitian TPS restoration.
